confusing.title: The pairs that cost marks in ratio questions
rows: Current ratio vs quick ratio
Quick assets drop inventories AND prepaid expenses; benchmarks are 2:1 and 1:1
'Acid test' means quick
Operating ratio vs operating profit ratio
Operating ratio is costs over sales; operating profit ratio is EBIT over sales. They add to 100%
'Profit' in the name means the margin, not the cost
Cost of goods sold vs cost of sales
Only selling and distribution expenses separate them; in their absence they are equal
If selling expenses are given, the two differ
Capital gearing vs proprietary ratio
Preference capital sits in the numerator of gearing but inside the proprietary fund
Preference capital switches sides
ROCE vs ROE
ROCE is EBIT over capital employed (equity + long-term debt); ROE is PAT less preference dividend over net worth
'Employed' means everyone's money
Dividend percentage vs dividend yield
Percentage is on paid-up value; yield is on market price and is the true return
'Yield' always means market price
Interest coverage vs fixed charges coverage
Interest coverage is EBIT over interest; fixed charges adds depreciation on top and loan repayment below
Depreciation added means fixed charges
Horizontal vs vertical analysis
Horizontal compares years; vertical reads one year as percentages of sales and total assets
'Single year' means vertical
Intangible vs fictitious assets
Intangibles (goodwill, patents, trade marks) are included in capital employed; fictitious assets (deferred expenses) are not
'Deferred' means leave it out

cases.title: Integrated Case 1 — Sarita Textiles Ltd. under the lens
facts: Sarita Textiles Ltd. reports sales of ₹48,00,000, all on credit, with a gross profit ratio of 25%. Opening stock was ₹2,50,000 and closing stock ₹3,50,000. Opening debtors were ₹5,50,000 and closing debtors ₹6,50,000. Assume a 360-day year.

Its balance sheet shows current assets of ₹8,00,000, of which inventories are ₹3,50,000 and prepaid expenses ₹30,000, against current liabilities of ₹3,20,000 which include a bank overdraft of ₹40,000.
The long-term side shows equity share capital ₹8,00,000, reserves and surplus ₹2,00,000, 10% preference share capital ₹3,00,000 and 12% debentures ₹7,00,000. Total assets are ₹23,20,000.
Earnings before interest and tax for the year were ₹4,80,000; the tax rate is 30%. The company also carries deferred revenue expenditure of ₹20,000 on the assets side.
Sarita deals in cotton garments and holds four times its normal inventory from October to January. The financial year closes on 31st March, at the low point of that cycle.

questions.q: The quick ratio of Sarita Textiles Ltd. is:
reasoning: SM §3.1(b): Quick Assets = Current Assets − Inventories − Prepaid expenses = ₹8,00,000 − ₹3,50,000 − ₹30,000 = ₹4,20,000.
Quick ratio = ₹4,20,000 ÷ ₹3,20,000 = 1.3125, stated as 1.31 : 1, comfortably above the satisfactory 1:1.
Option C (1.41 : 1) is the figure you get by deducting inventories but leaving prepaid expenses in — the single most common slip in this chapter. Option B is the current ratio, ₹8,00,000 ÷ ₹3,20,000.

questions.q: The inventory turnover ratio, based on cost of goods sold, is:
reasoning: Cost of goods sold = Sales − Gross profit = ₹48,00,000 − 25% of ₹48,00,000 = ₹36,00,000.
Average inventory = (Opening stock ₹2,50,000 + Closing stock ₹3,50,000) ÷ 2 = ₹3,00,000.
SM §3.3: Inventory Turnover Ratio = Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Average Inventory = ₹36,00,000 ÷ ₹3,00,000 = 12 times, an inventory holding period of 30 days.

questions.q: The capital gearing ratio of the company is:
reasoning: SM §3.2.1: Capital Gearing Ratio = (Preference Share Capital + Debentures + Other Borrowed funds) ÷ (Equity Share Capital + Reserves & Surplus − Losses).
So the ratio is 1 : 1. Note that preference capital sits in the numerator here, but would sit inside the proprietary fund in the proprietary ratio.

questions.q: In computing return on capital employed, the deferred revenue expenditure of ₹20,000 should be:

options.A: Included in capital employed, like goodwill and patents
options.B: Added to earnings before interest and taxes

reasoning: SM §3.4.2: intangible assets such as goodwill, patents and trade marks should be included in capital employed, but no fictitious asset, such as deferred expenses, should be included.
The distinction is between an asset with no physical existence but real value (intangible) and an expense carried forward on the balance sheet (fictitious).

questions.q: The year-end inventory figure of a cotton-garment business whose peak season runs October to January illustrates which limitation of financial ratios?
reasoning: SM §6(iii): seasonal factors may influence financial data. The study material's own illustration is a company dealing in cotton garments which keeps a high inventory from October to January and only a quarter of that level for the rest of the year.

Consequently the liquidity and inventory ratios produce a biased picture, and the year-end picture may not be the average picture of the business. Monthly average inventory data would cure it, but external users rarely have it.

cases.trap: Every part here is decided by a definition, not by arithmetic: what quick assets exclude, which flow turns inventory over, which side preference capital sits on, and what counts as a fictitious asset.

cases.title: Integrated Case 2 — Two years of Hemant Industries Ltd.
facts: Hemant Industries Ltd. reports, for the year just ended: sales ₹55,00,000, direct costs ₹30,00,000 and other operating expenses ₹4,80,000. It uses total assets of ₹50,00,000, of which 35% is financed by debt carrying 10.50% per annum. The tax rate is 33%.
The company has 2,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each in issue and no preference capital. It paid an equity dividend of ₹2 per share. The market price per share at the year end was ₹75.
The previous year's figures, on the same basis, were sales ₹45,00,000, total assets ₹45,00,000 and profit after tax ₹9,00,000.
The board is comparing this year's statements with last year's, and separately wants each item of the profit and loss account expressed as a percentage of gross sales.
The company's banker has asked for the debt service coverage ratio. Depreciation for the year was ₹3,00,000 and the annual loan instalment is ₹2,00,000.

questions.q: Earnings before interest and taxes for the year are:
reasoning: EBIT = Sales − Direct costs − Other operating expenses = ₹55,00,000 − ₹30,00,000 − ₹4,80,000 = ₹20,20,000.
SM §3.4.1: operating profit = sales − cost of goods sold − operating expenses, and is often referred to as earnings before interest and taxes.
₹18,36,250 is earnings before taxes (after interest of ₹1,83,750) and ₹12,30,288 is profit after tax.

questions.q: The return on equity for the year is closest to:
reasoning: 24.61% is the return on assets and 22.37% the net profit margin; 40.40% is EBIT over equity, which is not a study material ratio.

questions.q: The price-earnings ratio at the year end is closest to:
reasoning: EPS = PAT ÷ number of equity shares = ₹12,30,287.50 ÷ 2,00,000 = ₹6.15 (there is no preference dividend, so SM §3.4.4 note 2 allows PAT to be taken as earnings available to equity shareholders).
SM §3.4.4: P/E Ratio = Market Price per Share ÷ Earnings per Share = ₹75 ÷ ₹6.15 = 12.19 times.
₹6.15 is the EPS itself and 8.20% is the earnings yield, the reciprocal expressed as a percentage.

questions.q: The debt service coverage ratio the banker has asked for is closest to:
reasoning: SM §3.2.2: earnings available for debt service = PAT + non-cash operating expenses + interest = ₹12,30,287.50 + ₹3,00,000 + ₹1,83,750 = ₹17,14,037.50.

DSCR = Earnings available for debt service ÷ (Interest + Instalments) = ₹17,14,037.50 ÷ (₹1,83,750 + ₹2,00,000) = ₹17,14,037.50 ÷ ₹3,83,750 = 4.47 times, or 4.53 on slightly different rounding of PAT.
The study material calls a DSCR of 1.5 to 2 satisfactory, so the lender's cushion here is wide. The examinable step is adding back depreciation and interest to PAT.

questions.q: Expressing each item of the profit and loss account as a percentage of gross sales is:
reasoning: SM §7: vertical analysis is the analysis of a single year's financial statement, in which every item of the profit and loss account is expressed as a percentage of gross sales and every balance sheet item as a percentage of total assets.
Comparing this year's statements with last year's, which the board is also doing, is horizontal analysis — the two are being carried out side by side.

cases.trap: Options are built from the other ratios in the same working: net profit margin, return on assets, EPS and earnings yield all appear as distractors for one another.

mcqs.question: A generally acceptable current ratio, as per the study material, is:
mcqs.explanation: SM §3.1: a generally acceptable current ratio is 2:1, though whether a specific ratio is satisfactory depends on the nature of the business.

mcqs.question: Net working capital, as defined in the study material, is current assets less current liabilities:
mcqs.explanation: SM §3.1(e): Net Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities (excluding short-term bank borrowing).

mcqs.question: The debt-equity ratio is described in the study material as the indicator of a firm's:
mcqs.explanation: SM §3.2.1(c): debt equity ratio is the indicator of the firm's financial leverage.

mcqs.question: Capital employed, for the purpose of ROCE, may be computed as all of the following EXCEPT:

options.D: Equity share capital + Preference share capital

mcqs.explanation: SM §3.4.2 gives the first three definitions; the fourth describes the proprietary fund, not capital employed.

mcqs.question: The average collection period can be computed as:
mcqs.explanation: SM §3.3(ii): average collection period = average accounts receivable ÷ average daily credit sales, or 12 months / 52 weeks / 360 days ÷ receivables turnover ratio.

mcqs.question: Operating profit ratio and operating ratio, as defined in the study material:

options.A: Are the same ratio under two names
options.C: Together account for 100% of sales, one being costs and the other the margin
options.D: Are both computed on capital employed

mcqs.explanation: SM §3.4.1: the operating ratio is (COGS + operating expenses) over sales and the operating profit ratio is operating profit over sales; both are struck before interest and taxes.

mcqs.question: Under the Du Pont model, an increase in return on equity caused solely by a rise in the equity multiplier means the improvement came from:

options.B: Faster conversion of assets into sales
options.C: A reduction in the tax rate
options.D: Returns earned on the debt at work in the business

mcqs.explanation: SM §3.4.2: the equity multiplier is a measure of financial leverage, allowing the investor to see what portion of the return on equity is the result of debt.

mcqs.question: Dividend yield, as per the study material, is computed on:
mcqs.explanation: SM §3.4.4: dividend yield = DPS ÷ MPS × 100; dividend percentage indicates return on paid-up value, but yield is the indicator of true return, taking share capital at market value.

mcqs.question: Which class of user is listed in the study material as relying mainly on coverage ratios?
mcqs.explanation: SM §4: lenders keep an eye on the safety of their money lent and use coverage, solvency, turnover and profitability ratios.

mcqs.question: 'Financial ratios provide clues but not conclusions' appears in the study material as the conclusion to:

options.B: The section on the sources of financial data
options.C: The section on the Du Pont model

mcqs.explanation: SM §6: after the eight limitations, the study material adds that ratios provide clues but not conclusions and are tools only in the hands of experts.

mcqs.question: A company has a current ratio of 3 and working capital of ₹6,00,000. Its current assets are:
mcqs.explanation: Working capital = CA − CL = 3 CL − CL = 2 CL, so CL = ₹3,00,000 and CA = 3 × ₹3,00,000 = ₹9,00,000.

mcqs.question: Sales are ₹40,00,000 with a gross profit ratio of 20%. Opening stock is ₹2,00,000 and closing stock ₹3,00,000. Purchases for the year are:

descriptive.question: From the following prepare the Balance Sheet: current ratio 2.5, liquid ratio 1.5, working capital ₹4,80,000, fixed assets to proprietary ratio 0.75, reserves and surplus 20% of share capital. Show working notes.
answer_points: **Current assets and current liabilities:** working capital = 2.5 CL − CL = 1.5 CL, so CL = ₹4,80,000 ÷ 1.5 = ₹3,20,000 and current assets = ₹8,00,000.
**Inventory:** liquid ratio 1.5 = (₹8,00,000 − inventories) ÷ ₹3,20,000, so inventories = ₹8,00,000 − ₹4,80,000 = ₹3,20,000.
**Proprietary fund and fixed assets:** 0.75 PF + ₹8,00,000 = PF + ₹3,20,000, so 0.25 PF = ₹4,80,000, PF = ₹19,20,000 and fixed assets = ₹14,40,000.
**Share capital and reserves:** 1.20 × share capital = ₹19,20,000, so share capital = ₹16,00,000 and reserves = ₹3,20,000.
**Balance Sheet:** share capital ₹16,00,000, reserves ₹3,20,000, creditors ₹3,20,000 = ₹22,40,000; fixed assets ₹14,40,000, stock ₹3,20,000, other current assets ₹4,80,000 = ₹22,40,000.

descriptive.question: Complete the Balance Sheet from the following: inventory turnover ratio (based on cost of goods sold) 7.5 times; total assets turnover ratio 2.5 times; long-term debt to shareholders' fund 0.6:1; debtors collection period 30 days; gross profit ratio 25% on sales; current ratio 2.9:1. Equity share capital ₹6,00,000, reserves and surplus ₹3,00,000, creditors ₹3,00,000. Assume a 360-day year and all credit sales.
answer_points: Present the Balance Sheet, both sides totalling ₹17,40,000, and state the assumption that all sales are credit sales.

descriptive.question: A company plans total assets of ₹50,00,000, with 35% financed by debt at 10.50% per annum. Projected sales are ₹55,00,000, direct costs ₹30,00,000 and other operating expenses ₹4,80,000. The tax rate is 33%. Compute profit after tax, the net profit margin after tax, the return on assets after tax, the asset turnover ratio and the return on equity.
Explain the four coverage ratios given in the study material, with their formulae and the benchmarks stated.
answer_points: Coverage ratios measure the firm's ability to service fixed liabilities — interest on loans, preference dividend, and amortisation of principal or redemption of preference capital on maturity.

**Debt service coverage ratio** = Earnings available for debt service ÷ (Interest + Instalments), where earnings available for debt service = EAT + non-cash operating expenses such as depreciation + interest + other adjustments. Normally a DSCR of 1.5 to 2 is satisfactory.

**Interest coverage ratio**, also known as the times interest earned ratio, = EBIT ÷ Interest. EBIT is used because the ability to pay interest is not affected by the tax burden, interest on debt funds being a deductible expense. A high ratio means interest obligations can be met even if EBIT declines considerably; a lower ratio indicates excessive use of debt or inefficient operations.

**Preference dividend coverage ratio** = Earnings after taxes ÷ Preference dividend; it indicates the margin of safety available to preference shareholders. Equity dividend coverage = (EAT − preference dividend) ÷ Equity dividend.

**Fixed charges coverage ratio** = (EBIT + Depreciation) ÷ (Interest + Repayment of loan); it shows how many times the cash flow before interest and taxes covers all fixed financing charges, and a ratio of more than 1 is considered safe.

descriptive.question: Explain any five limitations of financial ratios, and state what the study material concludes about their use.
answer_points: **Diversified product lines:** ratios on aggregate data of a multi-industry business cannot be used for inter-firm comparisons.
**Distortion by inflation:** historical cost values may differ substantially from true values, and the distortion is carried into the ratios.

**Seasonal factors:** a cotton-garment business holding high inventory from October to January and a quarter of that for the rest of the year produces biased liquidity and inventory ratios; the year-end picture may not be the average picture.
**Window dressing:** year-end adjustments made to flatter popular ratios change their character.
**Differences in accounting policies and accounting period** make two firms' data and ratios non-comparable.

**No standard set of ratios:** the industry average is a low standard for a firm that wants to be above average, and too high for one below it. **It is also difficult to generalise whether a ratio is good or bad** — a high current ratio may result from inefficient working capital management. **Ratios are inter-related, not independent**, which multivariate analysis addresses.

The study material concludes that financial ratios provide clues but not conclusions, and are tools only in the hands of experts, because there is no standard ready-made interpretation of financial ratios.

descriptive.question: Distinguish between horizontal and vertical analysis, and state which users of financial analysis the study material associates with liquidity ratios, coverage ratios and market ratios respectively.
answer_points: **Horizontal analysis:** the financial statements of one year are analysed and interpreted after comparing with another year or years; it can be based on the ratios derived from the financial information over the same time span.

**Vertical analysis:** the financial statement of a single year is analysed. Every item of the profit and loss account is expressed as a percentage of gross sales, and every balance sheet item as a percentage of total assets. It is useful in inter-firm comparison.

**Liquidity and short-term solvency ratios** are associated with creditors, who want to know whether the organisation will be able to pay on the due date; they are also particularly useful in credit analysis by banks and other suppliers of short-term loans.
**Coverage ratios** are associated with lenders, who keep an eye on the safety of the money they have lent, alongside solvency, turnover and profitability ratios.
**Market ratios — EPS, DPS, P/E and the dividend payout ratio — are associated with shareholders**, who as owners are interested in the profitability and growth of the organisation.

quick.a: Current ratio, quick or acid-test ratio, cash or absolute liquidity ratio, basic defense interval, and net working capital.

quick.q: Name the six capital structure ratios.
quick.a: Equity ratio, debt ratio, debt to equity ratio, debt to total assets ratio, capital gearing ratio and proprietary ratio.
Debt service coverage, interest coverage, preference dividend coverage and fixed charges coverage.

quick.q: Name the four categories of profitability ratios.
quick.a: Related to sales; related to overall return on investment; required from the owner's point of view; related to market, valuation and investors.

quick.q: Name the three components of the Du Pont model.
quick.a: Net profit margin, asset turnover and the equity multiplier.

quick.q: Name the six sources of financial data for analysis.
quick.a: Annual reports, interim financial statements, notes to accounts, statement of cash flows, business periodicals, and credit and investment advisory services.

quick.q: Name the four market or valuation ratios.
quick.a: Price-earnings ratio, dividend and earnings yield, market value to book value per share, and the Q ratio.

quick.q: Name the six aspects in which ratio analysis is relevant for assessing performance.
quick.a: Liquidity position, long-term solvency, operating efficiency, overall profitability, inter-firm comparison, and budgeting.

true_false.s: A high current ratio is always a good sign.
true_false.reason: SM §6(vii): a high current ratio may not be good, as it may result from inefficient working capital management.

true_false.s: Interest coverage uses earnings after tax in the numerator.
true_false.reason: It uses EBIT, because the ability to pay interest is not affected by the tax burden, interest being a deductible expense.

true_false.s: Preference share capital forms part of the proprietary fund.
true_false.reason: SM §3.2.1(f): proprietary fund includes equity share capital, preference share capital and reserves and surplus.

true_false.s: Intangible assets such as goodwill are excluded from capital employed.
true_false.reason: Intangibles are included; only fictitious assets such as deferred expenses are excluded.

true_false.s: A firm with old plant and machinery may show a higher fixed assets turnover ratio than one that bought recently.
true_false.reason: SM §3.3(b); the written-down value in the denominator is lower.

true_false.s: Vertical analysis compares one year's statements with another year's.
true_false.reason: That is horizontal analysis; vertical analysis reads a single year as percentages.

true_false.s: A very high working capital turnover ratio is purely a sign of efficiency.
true_false.reason: SM §3.3(e): it indicates that the company needs to raise additional working capital for future needs.

true_false.s: Dividend percentage and dividend yield are computed on different bases.
true_false.reason: Percentage is on paid-up value; yield is on market price and is the indicator of true return.

differentiate.a: Current: all current assets over current liabilities, benchmark 2:1. Quick: current assets less inventories and prepaid expenses over current liabilities, benchmark 1:1.
ROCE: EBIT over capital employed (equity plus long-term debt); must exceed the borrowing rate. ROE: PAT less preference dividend over net worth; the equity shareholders' return.

differentiate.q: Operating ratio vs operating profit ratio
differentiate.a: Operating ratio is (COGS + operating expenses) over sales; operating profit ratio is EBIT over sales. Together they account for the whole of sales.

differentiate.q: Capital gearing ratio vs proprietary ratio
differentiate.a: Gearing puts preference capital and borrowings over equity funds. The proprietary ratio puts the proprietary fund — which includes preference capital — over total assets.

Horizontal compares one year with another over the same time span. Vertical analyses a single year, expressing P&L items as a percentage of gross sales and balance sheet items as a percentage of total assets.

Receivables: credit sales over average receivables; a low ratio means liberal credit terms granted to customers. Payables: credit purchases over average payables; a low ratio means liberal terms granted by suppliers.

sections.title: Liquidity
points: Current ratio = CA ÷ CL · 2:1 generally acceptable
Quick ratio = (CA − inventories − prepaid) ÷ CL · 1:1 satisfactory
Cash ratio = (Cash and bank + marketable securities) ÷ CL
Basic defense interval = liquid assets ÷ daily operating expenses = days of cover
Net working capital = CA − CL (excluding short-term bank borrowing)

sections.title: Long-term solvency
points: Equity ratio = Shareholders' equity ÷ Net assets · Debt ratio = Total debt ÷ Net assets (above 1 is risky)
Debt-equity = Total outside liabilities ÷ Shareholders' equity · the indicator of financial leverage
Debt to total assets = Total debt ÷ Total assets · Capital gearing = (Pref. + debentures + other borrowings) ÷ (Equity capital + reserves − losses)
Proprietary ratio = Proprietary fund (incl. preference capital) ÷ Total assets
DSCR = Earnings available for debt service ÷ (Interest + instalments) · 1.5–2
Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest · Fixed charges = (EBIT + depreciation) ÷ (Interest + repayment) · above 1 is safe

sections.title: Activity
points: Total / fixed / capital / current assets / working capital turnover = Sales or COGS ÷ the asset
Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ Average inventory · Raw material = consumption ÷ average RM stock
Receivables turnover = Credit sales ÷ Average receivables · Payables turnover = Credit purchases ÷ Average payables
Days = 360 ÷ the turnover ratio · COGS = Opening stock + purchases − closing stock
Very high working capital turnover signals a need for more working capital

sections.title: Profitability
points: On sales: gross profit, net profit, pre-tax profit, operating profit ratios; expenses ratios (COGS, operating expenses, operating, financial expenses)
ROI = Profit ÷ Investment = Profitability ratio × Investment turnover ratio
ROA = PAT (or PAT + interest, or EBIT(1−t)) ÷ average assets · ROTA and RONA
ROCE = EBIT ÷ Capital employed (Total assets − CL) · must beat the borrowing rate · include intangibles, exclude fictitious assets
ROE = (PAT − preference dividend) ÷ Net worth · Du Pont: margin × turnover × equity multiplier

sections.title: Owner and market
points: EPS = equity earnings ÷ equity shares · DPS = equity dividend ÷ equity shares · Payout = DPS ÷ EPS
P/E = MPS ÷ EPS · the payback period to the investor
Dividend yield = DPS ÷ MPS · Earnings yield (EP ratio) = EPS ÷ MPS
MV/BV = Share price ÷ (Net worth ÷ number of shares)
Q ratio = Market value ÷ Replacement cost · 1 = equilibrium, below undervalued, above overvalued

sections.title: Users, uses and limits
points: Creditors → liquidity · Lenders → coverage · Shareholders → EPS, DPS, P/E, payout · Investors → all four families
Six uses: liquidity position, long-term solvency, operating efficiency, overall profitability, inter-firm comparison, budgeting
Eight limits: diversified lines, inflation, seasonality, window dressing, accounting policies, no standard, hard to generalise, inter-related
Clues, not conclusions — tools only in the hands of experts
